lessonTitle: General, Regional and Local Anaesthesia: Choosing a Technique

blocks.text: A 62-year-old woman is having a carpal tunnel decompression under local infiltration when she mentions that her lips feel numb and she can taste metal. The surgeon has just injected a fourth syringe. Choosing a technique is half of anaesthesia; knowing how much drug the body can tolerate is the other half.

blocks.markdown: **General anaesthesia (objective 1).** General anaesthesia (GA) is a reversible drug-induced state of unconsciousness with amnesia, analgesia and (when needed) muscle relaxation, with the airway, breathing and circulation supported by the anaesthetist. Classically three components are combined: *hypnosis* (unconsciousness), *analgesia* and *muscle relaxation*. A balanced technique uses different drugs for each, so that each can be used at a lower dose. It is delivered in three phases: induction (usually an intravenous agent, or an inhaled agent in children), maintenance (inhaled volatile agent or intravenous infusion such as propofol), and emergence (stopping drugs, reversing relaxants and removing the airway device).
The classic **stages of anaesthesia** were described by Guedel for ether and are still useful for understanding induction and emergence, even though modern agents pass through them quickly.

rows: Awake and conversant, reduced pain perception; ends at loss of consciousness
Loss of consciousness with disinhibited reflexes: irregular breathing, movement, vomiting, laryngospasm; passed through rapidly
Regular breathing, loss of reflexes and relaxation adequate for surgery
Respiratory and cardiovascular failure from excessive depth
blocks.caption: Guedel stages of anaesthesia. Stage 2 is a danger period: avoid airway stimulation during induction and emergence.

blocks.title: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)
blocks.text: The alveolar concentration of an inhaled agent at 1 atmosphere that prevents movement in 50% of patients in response to a standard surgical incision. It is a measure of potency: the lower the MAC, the more potent the agent. MAC values of different agents (and of nitrous oxide) are approximately additive and fall with age; exact values vary by source.

rows: Rapid onset of unconsciousness; propofol causes hypotension; ketamine is dissociative and tends to preserve blood pressure
Maintenance of anaesthesia; potency expressed as MAC; can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients
Analgesia, blunt the response to laryngoscopy and surgery; respiratory depression
Relaxation for intubation and surgery; require ventilation; reversed by neostigmine with an antimuscarinic or by sugammadex for rocuronium
Reduce side effects and opioid requirement
blocks.caption: Main drug groups used in a balanced general anaesthetic.

blocks.markdown: **Regional, neuraxial and local techniques (objective 2).** *Local infiltration* and *peripheral nerve blocks* place local anaesthetic around nerves outside the central nervous system. *Neuraxial* techniques place it around the spinal cord and nerve roots: a *spinal* (subarachnoid) injection puts a small volume of drug into cerebrospinal fluid below the termination of the spinal cord, giving dense, fast block; an *epidural* places drug (usually via a catheter) outside the dura, giving a slower, segmental and extendable block. Neuraxial block blocks sympathetic fibres as well as sensory and motor, which explains the characteristic hypotension and bradycardia, particularly with a high block. Contraindications include patient refusal, coagulopathy or recent anticoagulant dosing that does not meet local timing rules, infection at the needle site or sepsis, raised intracranial pressure, and fixed cardiac output states (relative). Complications include hypotension, post-dural puncture headache, urinary retention, nerve injury, and the rare but serious epidural haematoma or abscess.

rows: Long, major or airway-sensitive surgery; patients unable to cooperate
Reliable unconsciousness, controlled airway and ventilation
Airway instrumentation, haemodynamic effects of drugs, nausea, slower recovery
Lower abdominal, pelvic and lower limb surgery
Dense block, avoids airway instrumentation, good early analgesia
Sympathetic block and hypotension, limited duration, headache, contraindicated by coagulopathy
Labour, major abdominal surgery, prolonged analgesia
Slower onset, patchy block, hypotension, dural puncture, haematoma risk
Targeted analgesia, opioid sparing, preserves consciousness
Block failure, nerve injury, local anaesthetic toxicity
blocks.caption: Comparison of general, neuraxial and regional techniques. The choice depends on the patient, the operation and local expertise.

blocks.markdown: **Safe maximum dose and toxicity (objective 3).** Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels. Toxicity follows from excessive plasma concentration, from rapid absorption from a vascular site, or from accidental intravenous injection. Dose limits therefore combine a weight-based limit *and* an absolute cap, and the lower of the two is used. Vasoconstriction with adrenaline slows absorption, which allows a higher limit. Quoted figures include plain lidocaine 3 mg/kg (maximum 200 mg), lidocaine with adrenaline 7 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg), and bupivacaine 2 mg/kg (maximum 150 mg). Check against current BNF and local guidance before any real use. A percentage concentration converts to mg per mL by multiplying by 10 (1% = 10 mg/mL).

blocks.caption: Take the smaller of the weight-based dose and the absolute cap; c is the concentration in % w/v.

blocks.title: Plain and adrenaline-containing lidocaine in an adult
blocks.prompt: An 80 kg adult needs infiltration with 1% lidocaine. Calculate the maximum volume with and without adrenaline, using the limits above (teaching example only).

steps.text: Plain lidocaine: weight-based limit is 3 mg/kg x 80 kg, then compare with the absolute cap of 200 mg.
With adrenaline: 7 mg/kg x 80 kg compared with the cap of 500 mg.

State the caveat: the cap, not the weight, limits an adult above about 67 kg for plain lidocaine; the adrenaline preparations are never used at end-arteries such as fingers; Check against current BNF and local guidance before any real use.

blocks.answer: Plain 1% lidocaine: 20 mL (200 mg). With adrenaline: 50 mL (500 mg), subject to the BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: When the absolute cap applies to bupivacaine
blocks.prompt: A 90 kg adult is to have a nerve block with 0.5% bupivacaine. Calculate the maximum volume using 2 mg/kg and a 150 mg cap (teaching example only).

steps.text: Total dose across all injections (including infiltration by the surgeon) must be counted; Check against current BNF and local guidance before any real use.

blocks.answer: A maximum of 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine (150 mg); the cap, not the weight, applies. Check the BNF.

blocks.title: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
blocks.text: Early features are perioral numbness or tingling, a metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness and agitation, progressing to seizures, then loss of consciousness, cardiac arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse. Bupivacaine is more cardiotoxic than lidocaine. Management (Association of Anaesthetists guidance; check the current version): stop injecting, call for help, give 100% oxygen, treat seizures, and give 20% lipid emulsion for cardiovascular compromise or arrest, following current advanced life support principles.

items: Stop injecting and call for help immediately.
Maintain the airway and give 100% oxygen; consider ventilation.
Control seizures with a benzodiazepine, avoiding large doses of propofol in an unstable patient.
If cardiac arrest, start CPR and give lipid emulsion per current guidance; prolonged resuscitation may be needed.

points: General anaesthesia combines hypnosis, analgesia and muscle relaxation; stage 2 is the dangerous excitement phase seen on induction and emergence.
The main drug groups are intravenous induction agents, volatile agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers and adjuncts; MAC measures volatile potency.
Neuraxial and regional techniques avoid airway instrumentation but cause sympathetic block, and are contraindicated by coagulopathy, sepsis at the site and refusal.
Local anaesthetic dose is the smaller of the mg/kg limit and the absolute cap; adrenaline permits a higher limit. Always check the BNF and local guidance.
LAST begins with perioral numbness and tinnitus; stop the injection, call for help, and treat with oxygen, seizure control and lipid emulsion.

questions.stem: During induction a patient develops irregular breathing, limb movements and breath-holding, with a risk of laryngospasm if the airway is stimulated. Which stage of anaesthesia is this?

distractorRationale.a: Stage 4 is overdose with respiratory failure.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: loss of consciousness with disinhibited reflexes is the excitement stage.
distractorRationale.c: In stage 3 breathing is regular and reflexes are lost.
distractorRationale.d: In stage 1 the patient is still conscious.

questions.explanation: Stage 2 follows loss of consciousness and is characterised by irregular breathing, movement and exaggerated airway reflexes. It is passed through quickly with modern drugs, and airway stimulation during induction or emergence is avoided.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a drug with its group?

distractorRationale.a: Rocuronium is a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker.
distractorRationale.c: Sevoflurane is a volatile inhaled anaesthetic.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: propofol is an intravenous induction and maintenance agent.

questions.explanation: A balanced general anaesthetic combines hypnotics, opioids and neuromuscular blockers, each with its own role. Knowing which group a drug belongs to explains its main effects and adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is scheduled for a knee arthroscopy under spinal anaesthesia. Which of the following would be a contraindication?

options.text: A body mass index of 31 kg/m2
A clinically significant coagulopathy (markedly raised INR)

questions.correctOptionText: A clinically significant coagulopathy (markedly raised INR)

distractorRationale.b: Obesity may make the block technically harder but is not a contraindication.
distractorRationale.c: Controlled asthma is not a contraindication; spinal can be advantageous.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: coagulopathy risks spinal or epidural haematoma and cord compression.

questions.explanation: Bleeding into the closed spinal canal can compress the cord, so impaired coagulation or recent anticoagulant dosing outside local timing rules prevents a neuraxial block. Other contraindications include refusal, local infection or sepsis, and raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: Shortly after a high spinal anaesthetic for a Caesarean section the patient's blood pressure falls to 78/40 mmHg and heart rate to 48/min. What is the principal mechanism?

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from the lithotomy position
Direct myocardial depression by local anaesthetic in the epidural space
Allergic reaction to the skin preparation
Blockade of sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilatation and (with a high block) loss of cardiac accelerator fibres

questions.correctOptionText: Blockade of sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilatation and (with a high block) loss of cardiac accelerator fibres

distractorRationale.a: Not the commonest explanation, and the timing fits the block.
distractorRationale.b: Systemic local anaesthetic effects occur after intravascular injection, not a typical spinal.
distractorRationale.c: Skin antiseptic allergy does not typically present this way.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: sympathetic block lowers vascular tone and can slow the heart.

questions.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres are blocked more extensively than sensory ones, producing vasodilatation and venous pooling; a block reaching the cardiac accelerator fibres adds bradycardia. Treatment includes oxygen, fluids, a vasopressor, and a vagolytic, with positioning as appropriate.

questions.stem: Which feature is typically an early sign of systemic local anaesthetic toxicity in a conscious patient?

options.text: A sudden fall in end-tidal CO2 with absent breath sounds
Profound bradycardia with a wide QRS and no warning symptoms
Perioral numbness or tingling with a metallic taste

questions.correctOptionText: Perioral numbness or tingling with a metallic taste

distractorRationale.a: Suggests an airway or circulatory problem, not typical early LAST.
distractorRationale.b: Arrhythmia is a late and severe feature.
distractorRationale.c: Cardiac signs can occur early with bupivacaine but are not the typical first warning.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: central nervous system symptoms precede cardiac effects in many cases.

questions.explanation: Rising plasma concentrations first affect the central nervous system, causing perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus and agitation, then seizures and coma. Cardiovascular toxicity follows, which is why a conscious patient's early complaints are treated as a warning to stop injecting.

questions.stem: Adding adrenaline to lidocaine slows its systemic absorption, which is why a higher maximum dose is quoted for lidocaine with adrenaline than for plain lidocaine.
questions.explanation: Adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction, so less drug reaches the circulation at any moment and plasma peaks are lower. The quoted limits (for example 7 mg/kg with adrenaline versus 3 mg/kg plain, subject to absolute caps) should always be checked against the BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 55 kg adult is to receive infiltration with 0.5% plain lidocaine. Using a limit of 3 mg/kg (absolute cap 200 mg, which you should check applies), calculate the maximum volume of 0.5% solution in mL. Teaching example only; check the BNF.
questions.explanation: The weight-based dose is 3 x 55 = 165 mg, which is below the 200 mg cap, so 165 mg applies. A 0.5% solution contains 5 mg/mL, so the volume is 165 / 5 = 33 mL.

questions.stem: A 60 kg adult is to receive a nerve block with 0.25% bupivacaine. Using 2 mg/kg with an absolute cap of 150 mg (check the BNF), calculate the maximum volume of 0.25% solution in mL.
questions.explanation: The weight-based dose is 2 x 60 = 120 mg, below the 150 mg cap, so 120 mg applies. A 0.25% solution is 2.5 mg/mL, so the volume is 120 / 2.5 = 48 mL; any other injections count towards the total.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is having an ultrasound-guided brachial plexus block with bupivacaine. Within a minute of the injection he becomes agitated, complains of ringing in the ears and then has a generalised seizure. Explain the diagnosis and outline immediate management.
markingGuide: Diagnosis: local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, probably from intravascular injection or rapid absorption
Early features (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation) precede seizure
Stop injecting and call for help
Maintain the airway, give 100% oxygen, ventilate if needed
Lipid emulsion for cardiovascular compromise or arrest (20% lipid per current guidance)
Prolonged CPR if arrest, and recognition that bupivacaine is cardiotoxic
questions.explanation: Prompt recognition and basic resuscitation are the foundation of treatment; lipid emulsion is a specific antidote for cardiovascular toxicity. Always follow the current Association of Anaesthetists guidance.

questions.stem: Compare spinal anaesthesia with general anaesthesia for lower limb surgery, covering advantages, disadvantages and contraindications.
markingGuide: Spinal: avoids airway instrumentation and controlled ventilation, dense block, good early analgesia
Spinal: sympathetic block and hypotension, headache, limited duration, failure
Contraindications: coagulopathy or anticoagulants, local infection or sepsis, refusal, raised intracranial pressure
General: unconscious, secure airway and controlled ventilation, suited to longer or major surgery
General: airway risks, haemodynamic effects of drugs, nausea, slower recovery
Choice depends on patient preference, comorbidity, surgery and local expertise
questions.explanation: Neither technique is universally superior; the choice weighs physiological effects against practical and patient factors. A shared decision is the usual approach.
